title: Major joint dislocation with neurovascular compromise
subtitle: Examine, reduce, re-examine, image the artery

sources.title: BOAST: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma

sources.org: Mills WJ et al. J Trauma 56:1261
sources.title: The value of the ankle-brachial index for diagnosing arterial injury after knee dislocation: a prospective study

sources.org: European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS), Wahlgren CM et al. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 69:179

red_flags.text: Knee dislocation, including the one that reduced before arrival and presents as a multiligament knee injury. Popliteal artery injury occurs even with palpable pulses.
A pulse that is absent, weaker than the other side, or a cool pale limb.
Skin tented or blanched over a fracture-dislocation, typically the ankle. The skin will necrose if it waits for the next list.
Posterior hip dislocation, particularly with a sciatic nerve deficit or a femoral head fracture.
Elbow dislocation with a brachial artery, median or ulnar nerve deficit.
Anterior shoulder dislocation in an older patient with an expanding axillary swelling: axillary artery injury.

do_now.text: Examine and document arterial and peripheral nerve function, with times, before any manipulation.
Reduce or realign a deformed, pulseless limb urgently, with adequate analgesia or sedation, then splint.
Repeat and document the arterial and neurological examination after reduction and after splinting.
If the pulse still does not feel the same as the uninjured side after reduction, treat it as an arterial injury: consultant input and CT angiography.
Perform procedural sedation in a monitored area with airway skills present.

assess.text: After a knee dislocation, measure the ankle-brachial index once reduced. An index below 0.9 needs CT angiography; a normal index with normal pulses supports observation with serial examination.
Hip: sciatic nerve, particularly the peroneal division, and the ipsilateral femur and knee.
Elbow: radial pulse, median, ulnar and radial nerve function, and the forearm compartments.
Shoulder: axillary nerve by deltoid contraction; the patch of sensation over the deltoid is an unreliable test.
Obtain radiographs before reduction unless waiting would harm skin or perfusion; then reduce first.

investigate.text: Radiographs in two planes before and after reduction.
CT after hip reduction to confirm a concentric joint and look for intra-articular fragments and acetabular or femoral head fractures.
CT angiography for a persistent pulse deficit after reduction, or an abnormal ankle-brachial index after knee dislocation.

resuscitate.text: Control external bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet applied as distally as possible. Do not clamp blindly.

definitive.text: A joint that cannot be reduced closed, or will not stay reduced, goes to theatre for open reduction.
Reduce a dislocated hip as an emergency; delay is associated with avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Confirmed arterial injury: revascularisation as an emergency, commenced within one hour of arrival, with a temporary shunt and skeletal stabilisation such as a spanning external fixator.
Vascular repair or interposition grafting by a vascular surgeon, with fasciotomy considered after revascularisation.
Do not rely on capillary return or a Doppler signal to exclude arterial injury.

escalate.text: Vascular surgery at the same time as orthopaedics for any dysvascular limb after reduction.
New or worse nerve deficit after reduction: senior review the same day, and a peripheral nerve service referral.
Multiligament knee reconstruction is a specialist, delayed procedure; arrange the referral before discharge.

notes: Document the neurovascular examination before you touch the joint. A deficit found only after reduction cannot be attributed, and the question will be asked.
A 'reduced' knee dislocation is still a knee dislocation. Ligament laxity in three or more directions is the clue.
Doppler signals persist distal to an intimal flap. The ankle-brachial index is the screening test, not the presence of a signal.
